name: Abraham
info: Abraham is the patriarch of the Book of Genesis, revered in Judaism, Christianity and Islam as father of the Jewish and Arab peoples; most scholars treat the patriarchal age as a late literary construct.

facts.born: In the Book of Genesis, in Ur of the Chaldees, the son of Terah; some exegetes such as Nahmanides place his birth in Haran; no date is given
facts.died: According to Genesis at age 175, buried in the cave of Machpelah near Hebron beside Sarah by his sons Isaac and Ishmael
facts.role: In Judaism the ethnic ancestor and first Hebrew patriarch; in Christianity the forebear of Jesus and the spiritual ancestor of all Christians; in Islam a prophet in the chain from Adam to Muhammad
facts.known: the call to leave Haran for Canaan; the covenant with God; Hagar and Ishmael; the birth of Isaac; the binding of Isaac; the purchase of the Cave of the Patriarchs

t: In Genesis, God calls Abram to leave his father's house for Canaan and promises him descendants and land; he is later renamed Abraham, meaning father of a multitude.
Jews hold him as the ancestor of the covenant, Christians as the spiritual father of believers, and Muslims as a prophet and the first to proclaim the oneness of God.
Most historians no longer regard the patriarchal narratives as historical, and many believe the Abraham traditions developed orally before entering Genesis in the Persian period.
dyk: In the Quran Abraham is mentioned in 35 chapters, more often than any other biblical personage apart from Moses.
ev: Terah's family leaves Ur of the Chaldees for Canaan and settles in Haran
At 75 Abram leaves Haran with Sarai and Lot and travels to Shechem in Canaan
He rescues Lot from the Elamite army and is blessed by Melchizedek
Hagar bears Ishmael when Abram is 86
At 99 he is renamed Abraham and receives the covenant of circumcision
Isaac is born and Hagar and Ishmael are sent away
The binding of Isaac in the land of Moriah
He dies at 175 and is buried in the cave of Machpelah

sections.early:
The Book of Genesis introduces Abram, later called Abraham, as the son of Terah, ninth in descent from Noah, and brother of Nahor and Haran. Haran, the father of Lot, died in Ur of the Chaldees while Terah was alive. Abram married Sarah, called Sarai at first, but unlike Nahor and his wife Milcah they were childless. Genesis records that Terah, Abram, Sarai and Lot set out for Canaan but settled at a place named Haran, where Terah died at 205. According to some exegetes, such as Nahmanides, Abram was actually born in Haran and later moved to Ur.

Scholars treat this world differently from the text. In the early and middle 20th century scholars such as William F. Albright and John Bright believed the patriarchs were real individuals or composites who lived in the 2nd millennium BCE. In the 1970s Thomas L. Thompson and John Van Seters argued that the stories reflect conditions of the 1st millennium BCE, and most scholars now see the patriarchal age as a late literary construct, though the stories may retain some historical qualities. Some scholars, among them Daniel Fleming, see parallels with the Amorite culture attested at Mari, and Alan Millard holds that the name Abram is Amorite.
sections.rise:
In Genesis 12, God tells Abram to leave his country and kindred for a land that God will show him, promising to make of him a great nation, to bless him and to make his name great. Abram was 75 when he left Haran with Sarai, his nephew Lot and their people, and he travelled to Shechem in Canaan, where he built an altar, and then to a place between Bethel and Ai. When a famine struck Canaan he went to Egypt, where he told Sarai to say she was his sister, and Pharaoh took her into his palace until plagues afflicted his household and he sent the couple away.

Abram and Lot, whose herds had grown too large for the same pastures, separated. Lot settled in the plain of the Jordan near Sodom and Abram went to Hebron, at the plain of Mamre. When Elamite forces took Lot captive, Abram gathered 318 trained servants, pursued them north and rescued Lot by a night raid. On his return Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of El Elyon, brought him bread and wine and blessed him, and Abram gave him a tenth of everything. In a vision, God again promised him a son and descendants as numerous as the stars, and made a covenant with him.
sections.deeds:
After ten years in Canaan Sarai gave her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram, and Hagar bore Ishmael when Abram was 86. When Abram was 99, God appeared again, renamed him Abraham, meaning father of a multitude, renamed Sarai as Sarah, and gave him the covenant of circumcision, which Abraham performed that day on every male of his household, himself and Ishmael included. Not long after, three visitors came to his tent at Mamre and told him Sarah would have a son in the following year; Sarah laughed. The visitors went on to judge Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abraham pleaded with God that the cities be spared if ten righteous people were found there.

Isaac was born when Abraham was "an hundred years old", and he was circumcised at eight days. Sarah then told Abraham to send away Hagar and Ishmael, and Abraham did so after God told him that Ishmael would also be the father of a nation. At some point in Isaac's youth, God commanded Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice in the land of Moriah; an angel stopped him at the last moment and a ram was sacrificed in the son's place. Abraham made agreements with King Abimelech at Gerar and Beersheba. When Sarah died he bought the cave of Machpelah near Hebron from Ephron the Hittite as her tomb. He took another wife, Keturah, and had six more sons.
sections.opponents:
The Genesis stories do not name an enemy of Abraham. His trials come as crises that threaten the promise: Sarah's childlessness, the famine, the capture of Lot, and the command to give up Isaac. The narrative also contains episodes that readers have found hard. Abraham presents Sarah twice as his sister, once to Pharaoh and once to Abimelech, who was warned in a dream and returned her; when Abimelech asked why, Abraham said he thought there was no fear of God in that place and added that she was in fact his father's daughter. Hagar fled into the wilderness after Sarai mistreated her, and was later sent away with her son.

Later biblical texts show the tradition being contested. In the Book of Ezekiel, written during the Exile, those who stayed in Judah claim the land by inheritance from Abraham, and the prophet answers that they have no claim because they do not observe the Torah. The Book of Isaiah says Israel's history begins with the Exodus rather than with Abraham. Scholars infer that Abraham was a figure used by the landowners of Judah to support their claims against the returning exiles. Israel Finkelstein and Thomas Romer suggest that the oldest traditions were an Iron Age hero story and that he may have been worshipped as an ancestor at Hebron.
sections.last:
According to Genesis, Sarah died and Abraham buried her in the Cave of the Patriarchs, the cave of Machpelah near Hebron, which he had bought with the adjoining field from Ephron the Hittite. The purchase is told as establishing his right to the land. After her death he took Keturah, a concubine, and had six sons with her: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. He lived to see Isaac marry Rebekah, a woman from his own kin, and the birth of his twin grandsons Jacob and Esau.

Abraham died at the age of 175 and was buried in the cave of Machpelah, beside Sarah, by his sons Isaac and Ishmael. On his death Isaac received all Abraham's goods, while the other sons received only gifts. The promise of land and descendants passes to Isaac, while Ishmael is promised that he will be the founder of a great nation. In the Genesis account the tomb at Hebron remains the family burial place. Jewish tradition counts Abraham with Isaac and Jacob as one of the three whose names are joined to God in the phrase God of Abraham, God of Isaac and God of Jacob. Genesis also lists the nations that descend from him: the Israelites, Ishmaelites, Edomites, Amalekites, Kenizzites and Midianites, with the Moabites and Ammonites related through Lot.
sections.legacy:
In Judaism Abraham is Avraham Avinu, our father Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people and the one with whom the covenant began, and his story is read in the weekly Torah portions Lech-Lecha, Vayeira, Chayei Sarah and Toledot. Jewish legend tells that he broke the idols of the Chaldeans and was saved from Nimrod's furnace. In Christianity Paul taught that Abraham's faith, which came before the Mosaic law, made him the prototype of all believers, Jewish or gentile; Augustine and Martin Luther later called him the spiritual father of believers. The Roman Catholic Church calls him our father in faith, and several churches keep his feast days.

In Islam Ibrahim is a prophet in the chain from Adam to Muhammad through Ishmael, a hanif and a muslim, the Friend of God and the reformer of the Kaaba in Mecca, whose mission was to proclaim the oneness of God. Muslims also call him the father of Muslims. The Druze count him as the third spokesman after Adam and Noah, Baha'is as a Manifestation of God, and Mandaeans as an original Mandaean priest. He is regarded as the common forefather of the Arab people through Ishmael and of the Jewish people through Isaac. Artists such as Rembrandt, Caravaggio and Marc Chagall have returned to the sacrifice of Isaac, and Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling (1843) takes it as its subject.

summary: Abraham is the patriarch of the Book of Genesis, called by God to leave Haran for Canaan. Jews, Christians and Muslims each revere him, as ancestor of the covenant, father of believers and prophet. Most scholars see the narratives as late literary traditions.
references: Ronald Hendel, Remembering Abraham: Culture, Memory, and History in the Hebrew Bible (Oxford University Press, 2005)
Jon Douglas Levenson, Inheriting Abraham: The Legacy of the Patriarch in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam (Princeton University Press, 2012)
